candidates.label: Church of the Holy Sepulchre (traditional site)
candidates.support: Identified as Golgotha since the fourth century AD under the Roman emperor Constantine; archaeological work beneath the church has found a first-century quarry with rock-cut tombs consistent with a site once outside the city wall, which is the majority scholarly view, though the precise course of the wall in Jesus' time remains debated.

candidates.label: Garden Tomb / Gordon's Calvary
candidates.support: Popularized as an alternative site in the nineteenth century, partly on the basis of a rock formation resembling a skull nearby; most archaeologists date the tomb chamber here many centuries before the first century AD, which is a difficulty for its identification as the Gospels' 'new tomb'.

summary.text: Golgotha, "the place of a skull," is the site of Jesus' crucifixion. Matthew, Mark and John give the name Golgotha, and Luke calls it "The Skull"; John adds that the place "was near the city," and Hebrews says Jesus "suffered outside of the gate." Its precise location is not settled. The two most discussed candidates are the Church of the Holy Sepulchre, inside today's Old City, and the Garden Tomb, about 600 meters to the north. Some scholars propose that the crucifixion and the burial were at separate spots within the same disused quarry, west of the first-century city.

history.text: John's Gospel says that "in the place where he was crucified there was a garden," with "a new tomb" in it. Mark describes women "watching from afar" and a centurion "who stood by opposite him," and Luke says two criminals were crucified with Jesus, "one on the right and the other on the left."

Byzantine tradition, following fourth-century construction under the Roman emperor Constantine, identifies the site beneath the Church of the Holy Sepulchre; excavations have shown that the area was a stone quarry with rock-cut family tombs before Jerusalem's walls were later extended to enclose it, though the course of the city wall in Jesus' time is still debated. The Garden Tomb was proposed in the mid-nineteenth century, when visiting Christian scholars suggested that a nearby rocky escarpment, whose face resembles a skull, marked the place of the crucifixion. Most archaeologists date its rock-cut tomb chamber many centuries before the first century AD, a difficulty for identifying it with the Gospels' "new" tomb.

Today both candidates are visited by pilgrims and tourists. The Church of the Holy Sepulchre encloses under one roof both Calvary, which church tradition identifies as the place of the crucifixion, and the tomb it identifies as Jesus' tomb. The Garden Tomb, outside the Old City walls, keeps its rock-cut tomb chamber in a garden that a British Christian charity has owned and run since 1894.

scripture.textWEB: When they came to a place called “Golgotha”, that is to say, “The place of a skull,”
They brought him to the place called Golgotha, which is, being interpreted, “The place of a skull.”
When they came to the place that is called “The Skull”, they crucified him there with the criminals, one on the right and the other on the left.
He went out, bearing his cross, to the place called “The Place of a Skull”, which is called in Hebrew, “Golgotha”,
Therefore many of the Jews read this title, for the place where Jesus was crucified was near the city; and it was written in Hebrew, in Latin, and in Greek.
Now in the place where he was crucified there was a garden. In the garden was a new tomb in which no man had ever yet been laid.
When the centurion, who stood by opposite him, saw that he cried out like this and breathed his last, he said, “Truly this man was the Son of God!”

There were also women watching from afar, among whom were both Mary Magdalene and Mary the mother of James the less and of Joses, and Salome; who, when he was in Galilee, followed him and served him; and many other women who came up with him to Jerusalem.
Therefore Jesus also, that he might sanctify the people through his own blood, suffered outside of the gate.

politicalHistory.entity: Kingdom of Herod the Great (ruler: Herod the Great)
Ethnarchy of Judea, Samaria and Idumea (ruler: Herod Archelaus)
politicalHistory.note: The emperor Augustus did not grant Archelaus the royal title his father's will asked for, only "ethnarch." This area's drawn shape also includes Gaza and the coastal strip north to Rhinocolura; Josephus records that Augustus took Gaza itself, with Gadara and Hippos, from Herod's kingdom at his death and added it to the province of Syria, but since none of these is its own area on this map, Gaza's land and this coastal strip stay within the area around them.

politicalHistory.entity: Roman province of Judea (ruler: Prefects, e.g. Pontius Pilate)
politicalHistory.note: Luke links a census "when Quirinius was governor of Syria" to Jesus' birth, which Luke and Matthew place in Herod's days; the Jewish historian Josephus dates Quirinius's own census of Judea to this year. This map takes no position on how the accounts relate. This area's drawn shape also includes Gaza and the coastal strip north to Rhinocolura, which stayed in the province of Syria from 4 BC on (rule 4, as in the previous period's note).
